datasets.title: The IAS machine family, 1946–1960
datasets.blurb: Every copy of von Neumann’s computer, placed where and when it first ran. Its design reports were circulated freely, so the family spread by copying.
datasets.why: The storyboard named it in 2007–08: “Computer graphing of computer spread is ideal. Each computer was local to a position in spacetime and the design (genotype) spread through clear lines of transmission.” The IAS design is a clean case. Its reports were circulated deliberately, and its copies are dated, placed and documented. BESM appears on some lists of IAS-family machines but was an independent Soviet design, so it is shown and flagged rather than left out.

datasets.title: The spread of printing, 1454–1500
datasets.blurb: The first press in 57 towns, from Mainz to Lisbon, Stockholm and Cetinje, each linked to where its printer came from.
datasets.why: Printing is the IAS family five hundred years earlier: a method that spread by people carrying it from shop to shop. In fifty years it went from one town on the Rhine to presses from Lisbon to Stockholm and Buda, and it is the medium every later cultural lineage in the Graph, Paradise Lost among them, travelled through. The towns and dates are well recorded. Who trained whom is recorded for only some of them, so most links are drawn grey until they are checked.

datasets.title: SARS-CoV-2 lineages, 2019–2026
datasets.blurb: Every Nextstrain clade of the virus, placed where it was first detected and linked to the clade it came from, from Wuhan to the lineages of 2026.
datasets.why: A real phylogeny made in the present, by a virus everyone lived through, and recorded month by month as it happened. It shows the Graph's rules under pressure: a place is where a lineage was first detected, never where it began; lines end where a variant stopped being tracked; and recombinants have two parents. Scrub from 2020 to 2022 to watch Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Delta rise and end, and Omicron take over.

datasets.title: The Unix family, 1970–2026
datasets.blurb: Twenty-seven systems from Bell Labs Unix to macOS, Android and the BSDs, linked by code, by influence, and by merges of several lines.
datasets.why: Software shows heredity more plainly than anything else: code is copied, forked and merged, and the record of who took what from whom is unusually complete. It also shows what a family tree hides. Linux took no code from Unix, only its design, so the link is drawn faint and can be left out of a trace; macOS has two parents, NeXTSTEP and BSD; and System V Release 4 has four. Pick macOS, then turn off Follow influence links, to see which ancestry is code and which is ideas.
